screens.title: Two loops, two jobs
screens.prose: This is **nested cross-validation**. The **inner loop** runs inside one outer training set. The **outer loop** holds back one outer fold at a time, which the inner loop never sees.
screens.question: Which loop chooses $\alpha$, and which measures the choice?

options.text: The inner loop chooses $\alpha$ on each outer training set; the outer fold then scores that choice once
The outer loop chooses $\alpha$; the inner loop measures it
options.why: You swapped the jobs. The outer test fold must stay unseen by the choice, so the choosing happens inside.

options.text: Both loops choose $\alpha$, and we average the two choices
options.why: Only the inner loop chooses. The outer loop is the honest test of the whole recipe, choice included.

options.text: Neither: $\alpha$ is fixed in advance
options.why: If $\alpha$ were fixed, plain CV would do. Nested CV exists because $\alpha$ is chosen from data.

hints.text: Which rows must the choice never see?
The outer test fold plays the role of a test set.
Inner folds pick $\alpha$ using outer training rows only; the outer fold then scores the winner.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which rows act as the test set for the choice.

explain.text: In outer fold 2, the inner loop sees only the other outer folds and picks an $\alpha$. That $\alpha$ is refitted on those rows and scored on fold 2. Averaging over outer folds scores the recipe “tune, then fit”.

widget.solution:
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, KFold, cross_val_score

def nested_cv_mse(X, y, alphas, k_outer, k_inner, seed):
    inner = KFold(n_splits=k_inner, shuffle=True, random_state=seed)
    outer = KFold(n_splits=k_outer, shuffle=True, random_state=seed)
    search = GridSearchCV(Ridge(), {'alpha': alphas}, cv=inner,
                          scoring='neg_mean_squared_error')
    scores = cross_val_score(search, X, y, cv=outer,
                             scoring='neg_mean_squared_error')
    return round(float(-scores.mean()), 4)

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

def make_loans(n, p, seed):
    """Loans: spread over base rate (percentage points). x0 leverage +0.6, x1 interest cover -0.4,
    x2 sector risk +0.3, the rest pure noise; noise sd 0.45."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, p)).round(3)
    beta = np.zeros(p)
    beta[:3] = [0.6, -0.4, 0.3][:p]
    y = (2.5 + X @ beta + rng.normal(0, 0.45, n)).round(3)
    return X, y

def make_noise(n, p, seed):
    """Loans whose p signals are all pure noise: spread = 2.5 + noise sd 0.45, unrelated to X."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, p)).round(3)
    y = (2.5 + rng.normal(0, 0.45, n)).round(3)
    return X, y

widget.solution:
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, KFold, cross_val_score

def selection_gap(X, y, alphas, k, seed):
    folds = KFold(n_splits=k, shuffle=True, random_state=seed)
    search = GridSearchCV(Ridge(), {'alpha': alphas}, cv=folds,
                          scoring='neg_mean_squared_error')
    search.fit(X, y)
    inner_best = -search.best_score_
    nested = -cross_val_score(search, X, y, cv=folds,
                              scoring='neg_mean_squared_error').mean()
    return round(float(inner_best), 4), round(float(nested), 4)

screens.title: Edge case: every fold disagrees
screens.prose: Nested CV on 200 real loans, tuning $\alpha$ over 1, 3, 10, 30, 100. Each outer fold’s inner loop picked its own $\alpha$. Tuning on all 200 loans picks $\alpha = 10$.
screens.question: What do you report, and which model do you deploy?

options.text: Report 0.2002 for the recipe “tune α by 5-fold CV”; deploy the recipe run on all 200 loans, α = 10
Report 0.2002 and deploy α = 3, the most common choice
options.why: A vote over folds is not the recipe that was scored. Run the same tuning on all rows, which picks 10.

options.text: Report nothing: nested CV failed because the folds disagree
options.why: Disagreement is normal when the curve is flat. The outer mean still scores the recipe, whatever it picks.

options.text: Report fold 1’s 0.1572 with α = 3, the best fold
options.why: You picked the luckiest fold. Report the mean over all outer folds.

hints.text: What did nested CV score: one α, or a way of choosing α?
Each outer fold applied the same recipe and got its own answer.
The score belongs to the recipe; the final model is that recipe run on all the data.

feedback.correct: Nested CV scores the procedure; the final fit uses the procedure on everything.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what each outer fold was testing.

explain.text: Every outer fold ran the same recipe, so their mean, 0.2002, is the recipe’s score. Different picks just say the curve is flat between 1 and 10. Running the recipe on all 200 loans gives the model to ship, here $\alpha = 10$.

screens.title: The nested estimate
screens.prose: Let $\hat\alpha_j$ be the setting the inner loop picks on outer training set $j$, and $m_j(\hat\alpha_j)$ its MSE on outer fold $j$. $$\text{nested CV} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^{K} m_j(\hat\alpha_j), \qquad \text{fits} = K(K_{\text{in}}G + 1).$$ The inner best uses the same rows to choose and to score, so on average it is lower.
screens.question: When is nested CV worth its cost?

options.text: Small data and a big search: say 300 loans and 40 settings
Large data and a small search: 50,000 loans and 3 settings
options.why: There a locked test set of 10,000 loans measures the choice cheaply and precisely. The selection gap is tiny anyway.

options.text: Always: it replaces the locked test set
options.why: It costs $K$ times a normal search. With plenty of data, a locked test set does the same job for one extra score.

options.text: Never: the gap is always about 1%
options.why: The gap grows with the search and shrinks with the rows. Our 105-pair search on 200 loans flattered itself by 10%.

feedback.correct: Small data cannot spare a test set, and big searches flatter themselves most.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weigh the size of the search against the rows available.

explain.text: Selection bias grows with the number of settings and shrinks with the data. With few rows, holding out a test set wastes data, and nested CV reuses every row. With many rows, one locked test set gives the same protection for one fit.

def count_fits(k_outer, k_inner, grid_size):
    return k_outer * (k_inner * grid_size + 1)

screens.title: Fifteen per cent better
screens.prose: A 30-feature credit model on 300 loans is tuned over a 10-point $\alpha$ grid. The grid’s best 5-fold CV MSE is 0.170. Nested CV on the same loans reports 0.200. The desk’s phrase: “the number you tuned on is not the number you report”.
screens.question: By what percentage of the nested score does the grid’s best number flatter the model?

hints.text: Take the difference, then divide by the nested score.
The difference is 0.030.

byKey.other: You divided by 0.170. Measured against the honest score, the flattery is 0.030 / 0.200 = 15%.
byKey.raw: That is the gap in MSE units, 0.030. Express it as a share of 0.200.

explain.text: $(0.200 - 0.170)/0.200 = 0.15$. A gap that large says the search had a lot of freedom for 300 rows. The model card reports 0.200, and the desk discounts any tuned number it is shown without one.

quiz.prose: An analyst runs `GridSearchCV` on all 400 loans, takes the best $\alpha$, then runs 5-fold `cross_val_score` of `Ridge(alpha=best)` on the same 400 loans and reports it.
quiz.question: What is wrong?

options.text: Every fold’s test rows helped choose $\alpha$, so the CV score still carries the choice
Nothing: the second CV uses fresh folds
options.why: New folds of the same rows are not fresh. All 400 loans chose $\alpha$ before being used to score it.

options.text: It fits too many models
options.why: Cost is not the issue. The tuning saw every row, so no fold is a clean test of it.

feedback.correct: Tuning on all rows, then cross-validating the tuned model, is a leak.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which rows chose $\alpha$.

explain.text: Once all rows have chosen $\alpha$, every later fold has already influenced the model. Put the tuning inside the outer loop instead: `cross_val_score(GridSearchCV(...), X, y, cv=outer)`.

quiz.prose: A reviewer sees `KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)` used for both the inner and the outer loop and worries the folds coincide.
quiz.question: What does the shared seed do?

options.text: Nothing harmful: the inner KFold shuffles each smaller training set, so its folds differ from the outer ones
It leaks: inner folds equal the outer folds
options.why: The inner KFold splits only the outer training rows, a different, shorter list, so its folds cannot equal the outer ones.

options.text: It biases the estimate low
options.why: A seed fixes which random folds are used; it does not tilt the score.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what list the inner KFold shuffles.

explain.text: The outer KFold shuffles all $n$ row numbers; the inner one shuffles the $0.8n$ rows of an outer training set. Different lists give different folds. Distinct seeds read more clearly, but the result is just as valid.

options.text: The best CV score: with 40,000 loans the gap is negligible

feedback.correct: With plenty of data, a locked test set does nested CV’s job cheaply.

explain.text: Eight thousand test loans give a precise score, and tuning on 32,000 loses little. Nested CV earns its cost when data is scarce.
